🌐 CoinDCX has confirmed losing 15.99 million USDT through compromised wallet infrastructure after initially rejecting claims that nearly $16 million had been stolen from the Indian cryptocurrency exchange. The exchange said a failure in its automated deposit-sweeping service allowed cryptocurrency to accumulate at an address that customers continued using despite instructions to switch to newer wallets. CoinDCX absorbed the resulting loss and maintained that customer balances and active trading systems were not affected.

⚠️ The admission follows several days of disagreement between CoinDCX executives and blockchain investigators over suspicious transactions involving wallets linked to the exchange. On October 22, CoinDCX CEO Sumit Gupta rejected suggestions of another security breach, saying the flagged addresses belonged to infrastructure compromised in July 2025. He maintained that no funds had moved from current operational wallets into the addresses under scrutiny.

📊 However, the company’s latest statement confirms that deposits continued arriving at those addresses and that its own systems were responsible for transferring them to secure wallets when the automated service functioned correctly. Cisco Unified Communications Manager Cross-Site Scripting Vulnerability
https://sec.cloudapps.cisco.com/security/center/content/CiscoSecurityAdvisory/cisco-sa-cucm-xss-5mQn2U5z?vs_f=Cisco%20Security%20Advisory%26vs_cat=Security%20Intelligence%26vs_type=RSS%26vs_p=Cisco%20Unified%20Communications%20Manager%20Cross-Site%20Scripting%20Vulnerability%26vs_k=1

A vulnerability in the web-based management interface of Cisco Unified Communications Manager (Unified CM) and Cisco Unified Communications Manager Session Management Edition (Unified CM SME) could allow an unauthenticated, remote attacker to conduct a cross-site scripting (XSS) attack against a user of the interface.
This vulnerability exists because the web-based management interface does not properly validate user-supplied input. An attacker could exploit this vulnerability by persuading a user of the interface to click a crafted link. A successful exploit could allow the attacker to execute arbitrary script code in the context of the affected interface or access sensitive, browser-based information.

Cisco has released software updates that address this vulnerability. There are no workarounds that address this vulnerability.
This advisory is available at the following link:
https://sec.cloudapps.cisco.com/security/center/content/CiscoSecurityAdvisory/cisco-sa-cucm-xss-5mQn2U5z

While the rest of the world is talking about the Binance hack, something is happening in the U.S. stock market that could turn out to be far more important for investors.

Alphabet lost around 13% in a single trading session, wiping out nearly $500 billion in market value and leaving the stock roughly 30% below its 52-week high. Yet, at first glance, the earnings report itself looked very strong. Google Cloud more than doubled its revenue, demand for AI continues to grow, and Cloud's future contracted revenue has already surpassed $560 billion.

But the market looked beyond the headline numbers. Google's core advertising business grew more slowly than expected, and, more importantly, the company has now reported negative free cash flow for the second consecutive quarter. In the most recent quarter alone, the company spent roughly $9 billion more than it actually generated after all expenses. The reason is the same as before: massive investments in AI, data centers, and its own chips.

And this is where an important shift has taken place. For the past few years, seeing rapid growth in AI-related business was enough for the market to forgive almost any level of spending. Now investors are starting to ask a different question. Not how quickly AI is growing, but how much actual cash a company has left after that growth.

And the problem goes far beyond Google. Alphabet currently accounts for around 5% of the entire S&P 500 and more than 8% of the Nasdaq 100. The seven largest tech companies together make up roughly 35% of the S&P 500. Yesterday, around 80% of the companies in the index were up, yet the S&P 500 still ended the day lower, largely because of Alphabet's decline.

So the biggest risk right now isn't that Google has turned into a bad company. On the contrary, its business remains massive and continues to grow rapidly. The real risk is market concentration. If investors start reassessing AI spending across the other tech giants in the same way, a correction in just a handful of companies could drag down the entire index. And even someone who simply bought the S&P 500 for diversification could suddenly realize just how much of their money actually depends on a few technology companies.
